stories.headline: Colossus 2 heads for about 1.2 million Blackwells by year-end
stories.why_read: The biggest single AI build you keep bookmarking now has names, GPU counts, and a power figure attached.
body: Elon Musk laid out how the Memphis-area Colossus 2 campus is split up. Two buildings, Macroharder and Minihard, each have 220,000 GB300s configured for training, Gun Range is set to match them, and a fourth building, Spam, gets roughly 200,000 GB300s for inference with simpler networking. In a separate reply he said the site should have around 1.2 million Blackwells by the end of the year.

X's news summary puts the campus at about 946 MW, and the inference-versus-training split is the interesting design choice: training needs the fat, expensive interconnect, inference doesn't. Musk also said in another post you saved that orbital compute deployed per month probably passes terrestrial compute around the end of 2028, which tells you where he thinks the next build after this one goes.

stories.headline: A 20,000-run Monte Carlo puts 2027 Robotaxi revenue near $900M
stories.why_read: A rare attempt to put ranges, not vibes, on Robotaxi revenue, plus a Cybercab capacity thought experiment you bookmarked.
body: Larry Goldberg (@TeslaLarry) ran a 20,000-run Monte Carlo on Tesla's driverless Robotaxi business. His base case is about $900M of 2027 revenue, with a low case near $350M and a high case around $2.5B. He puts the odds of topping $500M at nearly four in five and topping $1B at a little under half. In the base case, quarterly revenue climbs from about $18M this quarter to roughly $540M in Q4 2027, an exit run rate near $3B a year.

He's upfront that the fleet, mileage, fare, and cost inputs are his own assumptions, since Tesla doesn't disclose them, and that fleet growth and the pace of new city approvals move the result most. On the supply side, a post you saved from Genma_Jp compares the 2,400 Cybercabs a week in the earnings deck with what 30-second and 20-second takt times would produce: 16,000 and 24,000 a week at 80% uptime. He calls it a thought experiment, not a prediction.

stories.headline: A CVSS 9.8 Linux TCP use-after-free, and Ubuntu and RHEL aren't patched yet
stories.why_read: Every Linux server that accepts IPv4 TCP runs this code path, and Go opens the risky listeners by default.
body: CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE team scores it 9.8, and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. Stable kernels got a four-line fix on October 11 and 15, but as of Saturday evening Atlas reported Ubuntu's tracker still said vulnerable on every release and Red Hat listed RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix. Red Hat raised its rating to Critical on October 30.

Anthropic's researcher reported it, and the company says Claude wrote a working exploit that runs commands as root on servers with a multipath TCP listener. The Go Security Team says Go programs open those listeners by default. Until a fixed kernel lands, the write-up suggests dropping TCP packets with IPv4 options, turning off multipath TCP if you don't use it, and patching multipath hosts first.

stories.headline: One shared ChatGPT link was enough to take over the account that opened it
stories.why_read: A clean, readable exploit chain from two harmless-looking features, already fixed but worth understanding.
body: Parameter's Mukul Goyal describes how a public ChatGPT share could run attacker JavaScript inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. The chain started with the HTML Preview feature, which runs code in a sandboxed frame on a different domain, and found a way across into the main chatgpt.com page. From there the payload could list the victim's conversations, read a private chat never shared with the attacker, and send it to an outside server.

The victim didn't have to install anything or paste code. Opening the link was the whole attack. OpenAI fixed it on October 26 and rated it P1. If you build agent UIs that render model-written HTML, this is a good case study in why a sandboxed frame isn't the same as isolation.

stories.headline: Karpathy had Opus 5.5 build a YouTube made only of videos HN recommended
stories.why_read: A two-hour weekend build that shows what talking-only engineering looks like now.
body: Annoyed by YouTube's recommendations on a Friday night, Andrej Karpathy asked Opus 5.5 on Saturday to build a YouTube clone from videos recommended on Hacker News. It downloaded HN's comments, ran Sonnet over them in a Claude Code workflow to drop spam, and narrowed things to 40K comments that point at 6,454 videos across 150 topics from 2007 to 2026. The result, HackerTube, has its own recommendations stored in the browser, no accounts, and a data export you can hand to your own agent.

The process note is the bigger story. Karpathy says he no longer reads or writes code or runs terminal commands; his only manual steps were making a Google Cloud API key, booting a VPS, and buying the domain. He uses Opus 5.5 on medium effort by default. The post hit about 1,400 points on HN.

stories.headline: OpenAI's Astra tops robot benchmarks, and Freda Duan calls it robotics' GPT-3 moment
stories.why_read: A general model beating dedicated robotics models is the scaling story you track, now with arms and grippers.
body: X's news summary says OpenAI's Astra, part of the GPT-6 lineup, leads public robot intelligence indexes, including Playground's aggregation of 16 benchmarks, and beats dedicated robotics models in simulation and real-world tests. Investor Freda Duan called it robotics' GPT-3 moment, and OpenAI's Will Depue pointed to how surprising the results from scaling general AI have been.

Critics note it still struggles with fine dexterity and that latency and safety are real-world hurdles. The broader signal is talent moving toward general models at labs like OpenAI and Tesla, which matters for how fast Optimus-style robots pick up new tasks.

stories.headline: GSLV F18 launches NVS-03 to bring NavIC back to full strength
stories.why_read: Not "India gets its own GPS" but a better story: rebuilding a system that slipped below its minimum.
body: Balaji Thotadri's thread, which you retweeted and bookmarked, corrects the viral framing. India has had NavIC for years, but it needs at least four working satellites to work on its own. A few older satellites lost their atomic clocks and NVS-02 couldn't reach its slot last year, so the system slipped below that minimum. GSLV F18's launch of NVS-03 on Friday night puts it on track to get back to four.

The reason it matters is satellite timing: maps, shipping, fishermen's alerts, power grids, bank timestamps, and defence all depend on it, and India was denied GPS data during Kargil. NVS-03 also carries an Indian-made atomic clock, where not long ago every one was imported. NVS-04 and NVS-05 are lined up next.

stories.headline: Claude and Grok API outputs start carrying hidden watermarks this month
stories.why_read: If you pipe model output into email, resumes, or docs, it'll soon be statistically tagged by default.
body: To meet the EU AI Act's machine-readable labeling rule, Anthropic expands watermarking to more Claude models worldwide from November 3, and SpaceXAI's Grok API will watermark outputs from seven models by default, including grok-4.7 and grok-4.20 variants, across all endpoints from November 7. The marks are subtle patterns in word choice that survive light editing, with limited opt-outs for teams.

The quality question is live on HN. Keyvan's post walks through the debate John Gruber started about whether watermarking degrades writing, and argues it probably does a little. Eric S. Raymond and others expect workarounds, like rephrasing through open-source models, to show up fast.

stories.headline: Five Qwen3.8-27B agents match a published harness on LiveCodeBench Hard
stories.why_read: A careful small-model agent result that's honest about what it does and doesn't prove.
body: The memdoor team-solve example has five small models solve a problem together: a planner, two ideators, a solver, and a manager, plus a repair worker. Each starts fresh and they talk only through files on disk, while a script, not a model, decides success. On the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, five passes each, it averaged 9.8 out of 10 against 9.6 for the original authors' harness and 8.0 for a single Fable 5 call.

The README is refreshingly blunt: ten problems is a tiny sample, 9.8 and 9.6 are the same number, contamination can't be ruled out, and the model ran on OpenRouter rather than locally. A run took a median of 40 minutes and $0.39, and all 50 runs cost $35.79.

stories.headline: A researcher says Anthropic blocks him for anything touching model training
stories.why_read: The anti-distillation fight is landing on paying users doing ordinary research automation.
body: HKUST PhD student Jiahao Shao says he never distilled Claude: his rollouts came from an open-source model, and Claude only submitted jobs and ran analysis. He says he was still tagged for training a competitor, and now anything touching RFT, SFT, or training larger models gets him blocked, downgraded from Opus 5.5 to Opus 5, or has the session killed.
His post passed 228K views and drew a long HN thread. It's one person's account, but it's a useful warning if your own agent workflows touch fine-tuning pipelines on a closed model.

stories.headline: SpaceX posts a record Q3 as AI revenue jumps 830%
stories.why_read: The Super Intelligence line is now bigger than Starlink connectivity, which says a lot about where Colossus fits.
body: Per X's news summary, SpaceX's adjusted EBITDA for the quarter ended September 30 rose 306% to $8.8 billion. Super Intelligence revenue was $7.6 billion, up 830% from cloud deals and compute capacity, while connectivity brought in $5.25 billion and launches $1.77 billion.

Musk is targeting $500 billion to $1 trillion of annualized recurring revenue by the end of 2027, backed by compute ramping to 20 gigawatts. nextbigfuture, which you retweeted, argues the Minihard builds moving up a month add about $3 billion of revenue in October and $5 billion in November; treat that as his estimate.

stories.headline: Neuralink's R1 robot places 1,024 electrodes, and Blindsight is engineering-ready
stories.why_read: Surgical robotics plus a vision implant that skips the eye entirely.
body: Neuralink's new R1 surgical robot inserts 1,024 electrodes, using cameras and sensors to steer around blood vessels while a neurosurgeon oversees it. Musk also said the Blindsight implant, which signals the visual cortex directly to bypass damaged eyes, is engineering-ready. It has held FDA Breakthrough Device status since 2024.
Reaction on X mixes hope from people with neurological conditions with privacy and ethics worries, while clinical tests for motor function continue.

stories.headline: AI agents now run the Allen Telescope Array from plain-English prompts
stories.why_read: Agentic AI doing real instrument work at 2.4 terabits a second, physics and Blackwells in one story.
body: At Hat Creek Radio Observatory, the Allen Telescope Array uses Nvidia's Holoscan platform to let AI agents point antennas, calibrate instruments, fix data errors, and analyze live radio streams from simple English instructions. It processes up to 2.4 terabits per second on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

As a proof of concept it detected a pulsar in the Crab Nebula in real time. No alien signals yet, and scientists still check candidates by hand, but the setup is meant to catch unusual technosignatures that older methods might miss.

stories.headline: Grok Bot passes 600,000 daily users as people share bot-team playbooks
stories.why_read: You're living this one; the numbers and the playbooks people are trading are worth a look.
body: X's news summary says Grok Bot, launched in beta on August 11, has passed 600,000 daily active users, with Musk calling it the fastest growth he's seen for any product. Users build persistent bots for real work like updating CRMs, clearing tickets, and spotting wasted spending, which it says saved SpaceX over $100,000 on unused software. It costs $30 a month.

One playbook you retweeted from Kacper Rutkiewicz: install Dr. Eggbot, give it Matt Pocock's grill-me skill, let it grill you about what you want, then build the bot. Setup and clear rules still matter, which matches what people describe for specialized bot roles.

stories.headline: OpenCode now takes your Claude subscription, and Theo drops his effort setting
stories.why_read: Two small changes that affect what your coding agent costs and how you run it.
body: OpenCode announced you can now use a Claude subscription inside it, so the open-source coding agent no longer needs separate API billing to run Claude.

Separately, Theo says he moved from extra-high to high effort on Opus 5.5 and finds it better almost all of the time. Karpathy, in the HackerTube post, says he uses medium. More effort isn't always better, and it's often slower and pricier.

stories.headline: Not every decision should go to the LLM
stories.why_read: A crisp systems argument for classifiers and reward models as the fast path in agent stacks.
body: Arpit Bhayani argues for System 1 decision models alongside LLMs. Classifiers, reward models, and extraction models handle routing, gating, and scoring, so the LLM isn't the decision engine for everything.
For an architect, it's the familiar move of putting cheap, predictable components in front of the expensive general one, applied to agent systems where latency and cost add up fast.

stories.headline: AWS's trailing revenue tops 476 of the S&P 500's companies
stories.why_read: A one-line chart that puts the size of the cloud business in perspective.
body: Charlie Bilello points out that AWS's trailing-12-month revenue of $161 billion is larger than the revenue of 476 companies in the S&P 500.
Set it next to SpaceX's AI compute revenue and Colossus 2's GPU counts, and the infrastructure layer is where the money is pooling.

stories.headline: India curtailed 8 TWh of solar in three months
stories.why_read: The bottleneck is wires and storage, not panels, a pattern that shows up everywhere solar scales fast.
body: Prafull Billore, in a post you retweeted, says India curtailed 8 TWh of solar power between April and June, leaving 11.5% of capacity unused.
The author's point is that India's bottleneck is the grid and storage, not production. The same issue is behind every argument for big batteries and transmission build-outs.

stories.headline: India approves a Delhi-to-Guwahati bullet train corridor
stories.why_read: Delhi to Varanasi in about three and a half hours would reshape travel across the Gangetic plain.
body: ANI reports the Northern Corridor bullet train has been approved, running Delhi, Agra, Kanpur, Lucknow, Ayodhya, Varanasi, Patna, and Guwahati.
Projected times include Delhi to Agra in 59 minutes, Delhi to Lucknow in 2 hours 12 minutes, and Delhi to Varanasi in 3 hours 33 minutes.

stories.headline: Lead the agents, and keep your brain fit
stories.why_read: Two posts you saved land on the same advice for engineers in the agent era.
body: Gergely Orosz notes Steve Yegge is usually proven right six to twelve months later, and quotes Yegge: "Having a fit brain will be a key differentiator in the new era. Just do more of [writing], every day."

Uncle Bob Martin shared a line from Proton's CTO: "Your job is not to use agents to help you write code. Your job is to lead the agents." Put together, the job is direction and judgment, and you keep that sharp by thinking on paper.

stories.headline: FSD eases a driver's anxiety, and an owner calls the Model Y L his best product ever
stories.why_read: The human side of Tesla's weekend, plus spooky Robotaxi riders in Austin.
body: A clip you retweeted from Yair tells the story of April Lockhart, whose driving anxiety eased with FSD, which even parallel parks for her. Separately, tyler hogge says the new, longer Model Y is the best product he's ever used.
Tesla's Robotaxi account also showed off Halloween "spooky riders" in Austin, and a Cybercab dressed up with Mr. Skeleton made the rounds.

stories.headline: Tim O'Reilly: the chip supply chain is a planetary superorganism
stories.why_read: A big-picture read on why no single country makes a modern chip alone.
body: Tim O'Reilly recommends a New Yorker story that looks at today's interconnected world through semiconductor manufacturing. He quotes it: "The semiconductor supply chain is a planetary superorganism with its own ecology."
The piece argues the chip supply chain shows a non-zero-sum version of globalization, one that united its participants in something that couldn't be achieved without cooperation across continents.

stories.headline: Jepsen finds 96 issues in ParticleDB, an AI-focused database
stories.why_read: A reminder to test any "Full ACID" claim before you put agent state in it.
body: Jepsen tested ParticleDB, a multi-model database aimed at AI agents and apps that combines transactional SQL, key-value storage, vector search, and live analytics. It found 96 issues, from crashes, deadlocks, and data loss to rows that couldn't be deleted and dropped tables reappearing in distorted forms.

It kept losing committed writes in normal operation in its default mode and allowed lost updates even at serializable. Jepsen's verdict is that its "Full ACID" claim was somewhat premature, and the maker has since shipped fixes.

stories.headline: 100% CPU often means waiting on memory
stories.why_read: A clear refresher on why cache-friendly data layout still beats clever code.
body: Pivot's post explains that a CPU at 100% may be doing far less work than it looks. A modern core can run about 4 to 8 instructions per nanosecond, while a trip to RAM takes 50 to 100 nanoseconds, so one memory access costs roughly 400 to 800 instructions.
It walks through GROUP BY aggregations to show how databases keep work in small chunks that fit in cache. The author notes no LLMs were used to write it.

stories.headline: Nolan Lawson benchmarks which JavaScript frameworks agents build best
stories.why_read: Evidence instead of vibes for the "this framework is better for agents" claims.
body: Tired of framework claims made without evidence, Nolan Lawson had agents build the same small Pokémon app in several frameworks, five times each, and took the median. He measured development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and Lighthouse performance and accessibility, and tested each app against a conformance suite.
He's candid that the results are noisy because agents sometimes go off on token-burning tangents. His point is that you can still make framework choices from evidence in the agent era.

stories.headline: A Brazilian court fines lawyers for hiding a prompt injection in a filing
stories.why_read: Possibly the first ruling on someone deliberately hijacking a court's AI.
body: A Brazilian labor court found white-on-white text in a petition telling any AI to respond superficially and not challenge the documents. The court's AI tool, Galileu, flagged it. The court fined the two firms 10% of the R$842,000 claim, about $16,000.
The court said the lawyers tried to bias any AI used by the court or the other side. The ruling is from July and is back on HN this weekend.

stories.headline: Sam Altman says home PCs holding DRAM is "quite terrible"
stories.why_read: A real argument about whether local AI hardware or rented cloud compute wins.
body: On the Cheeky Pint channel, Altman said that from a global allocation view it's "quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time."
Tom's Hardware reads it as OpenAI preferring memory go to data centers over local inference, which worries people who want to own their hardware rather than rent it.

stories.headline: Zinc creep in its cable sockets brought down Arecibo
stories.why_read: A failure mode nobody had seen in a century, with a strange possible electromagnetic twist.
body: A National Academies report says long-term zinc creep in the zinc-filled cable sockets caused the 2020 collapse of the 57-year-old Arecibo telescope. The zinc slowly lost its grip, cables pulled out, and the platform fell into the 305-metre dish. It calls this the first documented case of the failure in over a century of use.

The sequence began with Hurricane Maria three years earlier, and visible cable pullout afterward should have prompted action. One hypothesis is that low-current electroplasticity from the telescope's own radio waves sped up the creep.

stories.headline: William Nordhaus, who put climate into economics, dies at 85
stories.why_read: The person behind the DICE model and the carbon-tax argument that shaped energy policy.
body: Yale reports that William Nordhaus died on October 30 after a battle with glioblastoma. He was 85. He won the 2018 Nobel Prize for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis.
His DICE model weighs the economic costs of climate damage against the cost of cutting emissions, and he used it to argue for a carbon tax. He spent more than 50 years at Yale, including as provost.

stories.headline: A farmer planted mystery seeds from his attic and grew a seven-eared wheat
stories.why_read: A lovely Sunday story about forgotten seeds, genetics, and luck.
body: In the early 1990s, Parma farmer Claudio Grossi found an old sack of seeds his great-grandfather likely left, tossed them on a manure pile, and forgot them. They sprouted several wheats, one six feet tall with seven ears per stalk instead of one.
Its kernels were bigger than usual and came in yellow, black, red, white, and even green, sometimes on one stem. Smithsonian follows how he turned that oddity into a crop.
